title: The Timestomper
subtitle: File System Forensics — MAC Time Manipulation
narrative: A corporate whistleblower claims that a disgruntled sysadmin tampered with critical HR documents and financial reports to cover their tracks before resigning. The sysadmin's workstation has been imaged. Your job: find the tampered files and prove the timestamps were falsified.
learningObjective: Understand how timestomping works by comparing $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME attributes in the NTFS Master File Table (MFT). Recognize that anti-forensic tools modify SI timestamps but often leave FN timestamps untouched.

preQuiz.question: In NTFS, which metadata attribute stores the timestamps visible in Windows Explorer?
options: $FILE_NAME ($FN)
$STANDARD_INFORMATION ($SI)
$DATA
$OBJECT_ID
preQuiz.explanation: $STANDARD_INFORMATION stores the timestamps shown in Windows Explorer and most forensic tools by default. This is also the attribute most commonly targeted by timestomping tools.

preQuiz.question: What is 'timestomping'?
options: Encrypting file timestamps with AES
Deleting the MFT entry for a file
Modifying MAC times to hide when a file was really created or accessed
Compressing timestamps to save disk space
preQuiz.explanation: Timestomping is the deliberate modification of a file's MAC (Modified, Accessed, Created) timestamps to mislead investigators about the true timeline of events.

preQuiz.question: How many distinct timestamps does NTFS store for each file in the $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute?
options: 4 (Created, Modified, Accessed, MFT Changed)
1 (Last Modified only)
2 (Created and Modified)
3 (Created, Modified, Accessed)
preQuiz.explanation: NTFS stores four timestamps in $SI: Created, Modified, Accessed, and MFT Changed. Each captures a different aspect of the file's lifecycle.

preQuiz.question: Which Windows API call is commonly used by timestomping tools to alter file timestamps?
options: GetFileTime()
SetFileAttributes()
NtSetInformationFile()
SetFileTime()
preQuiz.explanation: SetFileTime() allows user-space programs to set the Created, Modified, and Accessed timestamps of a file. Timestomping tools call this API to falsify $SI timestamps.

hints.text: In NTFS, every file has two timestamp records. Most tools only show you one. Try comparing them.

Timestomping tools typically leave runtime artifacts or temporary logs behind in the user's home profile. Where on a Windows system does application-specific configuration and temporary data usually accumulate?

When all four MAC timestamps of a file are identical down to the second, that is almost always the fingerprint of a timestomping tool. A user-space tool that modifies file timestamps must itself be executed — and on Windows, applications running under a user account store runtime data and logs in a specific directory structure. What kind of leftover artifact might such a tool leave behind, and where would Windows place it?

debriefing.title: How Timestomping Works
debriefing.concept: NTFS stores two independent sets of timestamps per file: $STANDARD_INFORMATION ($SI) and $FILE_NAME ($FN). Timestomping tools like Timestomp.exe or Metasploit's timestamp module only modify the $SI attribute — because that is what Windows APIs expose. The $FN attribute, updated directly by the NTFS kernel driver, is much harder to forge and often retains the true timestamps. A mismatch between $SI and $FN is a red flag.
debriefing.realWorldTool: Tools like Autopsy, FTK Imager, and the Sleuth Kit's 'istat' command can display both $SI and $FN timestamps simultaneously. Analysts specifically look for this discrepancy.
debriefing.caseConnection: In this case, the $SI timestamps were all set to the exact same second — a telltale sign. The $FN timestamps, combined with the Security Event Log (Event 4663), confirmed the real timeline. The leftover .tmp file from the timestomping tool was the clincher.
debriefing.furtherReading: NTFS MFT structure, Sleuth Kit istat, Windows Event Log 4663/4664, Metasploit post/windows/manage/timestomp

postQuiz.question: Which NTFS attribute is most resistant to timestomping tools and why?
options: $DATA, because it stores the actual file content
$FILE_NAME, because it is updated by the NTFS kernel driver rather than user-space APIs
$STANDARD_INFORMATION, because it requires admin privileges to modify
$OBJECT_ID, because it is write-protected by default
postQuiz.explanation: $FILE_NAME timestamps are maintained directly by the NTFS driver and cannot be changed through standard Windows API calls. This makes them a reliable forensic reference point even after timestomping.

postQuiz.question: What is a reliable indicator that timestomping has occurred?
options: All four $SI timestamps are identical down to the second
The file extension does not match its magic bytes
The file size is larger than expected
The file has no owner assigned
postQuiz.explanation: When all four $SI timestamps (Created, Modified, Accessed, MFT Changed) are precisely the same, it strongly suggests they were set programmatically in a single operation — the hallmark of a timestomping tool.

postQuiz.question: In this investigation, what corroborating evidence confirmed the timestamps were deliberately altered?
options: The files had mismatched magic bytes
The files were encrypted with a suspicious key
The Windows registry showed anti-forensic software installed
A tool artifact (timestomp_log.tmp) was found in AppData
postQuiz.explanation: The timestomp_log.tmp file in the user's AppData folder was a leftover from the timestomping tool itself. It named both tampered files and the exact timestamp applied — the strongest evidence of deliberate manipulation.

postQuiz.question: Why were all four $SI timestamps on the tampered files set to the exact same second?
options: The file was copied from a USB drive, which strips timestamp variation
Windows sets all timestamps to the current time when a file is accessed
NTFS automatically synchronizes timestamps for files modified by administrators
The timestomping tool used a single SetFileTime() call that applies the same value to all four fields
postQuiz.explanation: Timestomping tools typically use one API call to set all four $SI timestamps simultaneously. This creates the 'all-identical' pattern that's virtually impossible during normal file operations.
